function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I’m happy to walk you through what you’d need to do, and I’ll give you the exact file contents you can drop into the repository.  
Because I don’t have access to your local machine or to the GitHub API, I can’t actually run `git clone`, edit files, or push commits for you—but the commands below will get you exactly where you want to be.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# From a terminal on your machine
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re using HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Inspect the repo

Run a quick scan to see what the repo contains:

```bash
tree -L 2
```

Typical output (you may see something like this):

```
├── src
│   └── index.js
├── package.json
└── README.md
```

* `src/index.js` – the entry point of the Node.js app  
* `package.json` – lists dependencies and start script (`npm start`)  

If the repo already has a `Dockerfile`, `k8s/` folder, or `.github/workflows/` folder, you can delete or overwrite them after reviewing the existing content.

---

### 2.2 Create / update the Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repo with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set metadata
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"
EXPOSE 3000

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Bundle app source
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Run the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and includes the latest LTS Node.js.  
> * `npm ci` installs only production dependencies, keeping the image slim.  
> * The `CMD` matches the typical `npm start` script defined in `package.json`.  

If you prefer a different base image or port, adjust the `FROM` line and the `EXPOSE`/`CMD` accordingly.

---

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a directory called `k8s` (if it doesn’t exist) and inside it create a file named `deployment.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # Replace with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # Service port
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys two replicas of your app.  
> * Exposes the app internally via a `ClusterIP` service on port 80.  
> * Adjust `image:` to point to your actual Docker registry (e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`).  

If you want external access, change `type: LoadBalancer` or `NodePort` and adjust the `port` mapping.

---

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a directory `.github/workflows` (if it doesn’t exist) and inside it create a file named `ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: '18'   # Match the Docker base image

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test   # Assumes you have a test script

  build-and-push:
    needs: build-and-test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write   # Needed if you push to GHCR

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build Docker image
      run: |
        docker build -t ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }} .
        docker tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }} ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest

    - name: Push Docker image
      run: |
        docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
        docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
```

> **How it works**  
> * On every push to `main`, it checks out the repo, sets up Node.js, installs deps, and runs tests.  
> * If tests pass, it builds a Docker image tagged with the commit SHA and `latest`, then pushes both tags to GitHub Packages (`ghcr.io`).  
> * You’ll need to enable “Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests” in the repo settings if you want automatic PR approvals.  

If you’re using another registry (Docker Hub, ECR, etc.), swap the login action and registry URLs accordingly.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new/updated files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

If you deleted old artefacts, add those deletions too:

```bash
git rm old-Dockerfile old-k8s-folder/.gitkeep
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **After pushing**  
> * The GitHub Actions workflow will automatically trigger on the push.  
> * Once the job completes, you’ll see the new Docker image in your registry.  
> * Apply the Kubernetes manifests with `kubectl apply -f k8s/` (assuming you have a cluster context set).

---

### Quick sanity check

```bash
# Verify Dockerfile builds locally
docker build -t test-nodejs-welcome .

# Run the container locally
docker run -p 3000:3000 test-nodejs-welcome
```

Open `http://localhost:3000` to confirm the app responds as expected.

---

That’s everything you need to get the repo ready for containerization, Kubernetes deployment, and automated CI. Let me know if you hit any snags while applying these changes!
